findings.title: A replica has no trust anchor for genesis: a hostile server can replace an existing group's entire chain (forged membership, revived kicks, time travel)
findings.detail: A1 accepts a genesis whose author is the record's OWN self-declared `service` pinned key; the only gate on group creation is S1, which is server-only. P1 keys the head per group_id inside the group's rows, and the kept sync rule 'absent from a completed manifest -> drop locally' (plus P3 and P2's own 'drop the group locally and resync from genesis') deletes that head with no signature required. Sequence: (1) server omits 'prod' from one completed manifest -> replica X drops group G and its head; (2) next manifest: Group{name:'prod', epochs:[genesis G']} with a fresh group_id, pinned={backup: the real backup pubkey (public), service: server key}, acl = anything (attacker admin, X as reader, a kicked key revived), author = service key; in mode S the server holds the DEK and re-encrypts so X decrypts fine; (3) X has no head for G' -> C1 accepts -> X authorizes 'prod' from a server-chosen ACL and (P5) never takes a roster from elsewhere. Variant without the drop: nothing binds name -> group_id on the replica and the record does not contain the name. Variant B: after the drop serve the REAL chain truncated at an epoch where a since-kicked reader was still a reader (the server can derive M_k from the old record's service wrap and keep an old ciphertext snapshot). A brand-new replica or an offline auditor is pure TOFU. This contradicts the headline threat-model claim 'cannot forge membership, kicks or rotations for replicas or auditors ... fabricate a new group ... harmless'.
findings.fix: (a) Replicas never forget: per-NAME tombstone (group_id, last accepted head hash, epoch) that survives drops; refuse and audit a genesis under a known name with a different group_id, or any chain that does not pass through the tombstoned head (or re-root past it via a recovery signed by the backup key known at that point); a re-grant resyncs by fetching the full chain and verifying THROUGH the tombstoned head. (b) Genesis carries len(name)||name in the signed layout and secret_aad switches to group_id so a chain cannot be relabelled. (c) Every verifier pins the backup public key out of band (server: meta; replica: --backup-pubkey or TOFU-per-authoritative-node with audit; auditor: input) and refuses a genesis whose pinned[backup] differs; later backup-key changes are chain-verifiable via A3. (d) State in the threat table that a fresh replica's first chain and every genuinely new group name are server-attested (TOFU).

findings.title: A client-supplied genesis can pin an attacker-controlled backup key: the group creator becomes the group's permanent chain root, invisible to any key-less verifier
findings.detail: Section 8 adds `CreateGroup{genesis: bytes}`. R1 checks only shape, A1 accepts author = an admin in acl, S1 checks the caller's flag and that acl keys are registered; nothing compares `pinned` to meta.backup_pubkey_ed25519 / service_pubkey_ed25519 (6.1's 'epoch_mode decides what CreateGroup pins' covers only the server-minted path). Sequence: service admin S creates 'prod' with pinned={backup: K_S (a second key S holds), service: real service key}, acl={victim admin V: rwa}. Everything passes; in mode S the server opens its wrap and serves normally; the operator's real backup key opens nothing in this group (disaster recovery silently broken). At any later time S signs kind=recovery with K_S: A3 (author == head.pinned[backup]) passes for server, replicas (P2 re-root: signed by THEIR head's backup key) and auditors; S can jump the epoch, set acl to anything, kick V, replace the service entry, and is a recipient of every generation by G4. 'The service-admin flag has no chain power' becomes 'a service admin owns every group it creates', and CreateGroup requires service admin.
findings.fix: S1 MUST additionally require a submitted genesis's pinned set to equal the server's configured set for epoch_mode (exact backup key; exact service key in mode S, none in mode E), refusing with Failed{reason:'pinned set mismatch'}. Replicas and auditors verify pinned[backup] of every genesis against the pinned root (finding 1c); a backup-key replacement is accepted only via a recovery signed by the previous pinned key, so custody is a verifiable chain from the pinned root.

findings.title: A rogue admin can starve every kick and every recovery: the 'allow' default's safety argument fails under an adversarial liveness race
findings.detail: 'Allow' is justified by two remedies, a surviving admin's kick and the backup recovery; both race the rogue on the head. Kick: legit admin L exports, re-encrypts everything under M_new, stages under (group, hash(rec)), submits. Rogue R (an admin until the kick lands) submits an acl epoch flipping its own w bit with c0/wraps/proof carried verbatim (R5): one signature. L gets EpochConflict; per S3 L must rebuild with 'its M regenerated', and because the stage key is hash(rec) (which covers prev) every staged row is orphaned, so L repeats the full export/re-encrypt/re-stage. R needs one signature per L attempt; nothing forbids no-op or rapid epochs. Recovery: C3 on the server requires prev == hash(head) exactly; R moves the head before the service admin submits, and every retry is another offline ceremony; no freeze exists. Any rotate including recovery-with-rotate: S4 refuses if a version written between export and submit is uncovered; R grants itself w in its spam epoch and keeps writing; the uncovered versions need M_new, which for a recovery lives on the offline machine. Risk #1 frames this as benign load, not as an attack by precisely the party the mechanism exists to remove. Net: the rogue key keeps silent persistent read AND cannot be removed, worse than the 'forbid' row of the design's own comparison table.
findings.fix: (1) Decouple the stage from prev: key it by a client-chosen stage id or by the `reencrypted` digest; on conflict a rotate re-signs the header and re-wraps to the new recipient set (M_new + fresh r, no re-encryption); drop 'its M regenerated' from S3. (2) Server-side liveness rules (not chain-verifiable, fine for liveness): refuse no-op acl epochs (acl == head.acl and pinned == head.pinned); per-author rate limit on non-rotate epochs; a per-group 'recovery pending' freeze a service admin can set that refuses non-recovery epochs (optionally writes) until a recovery lands or it expires. (3) On the server accept a recovery under the replica rule (signed by head.pinned[backup], epoch > head.epoch, prev naming any record since the last recovery) so interim epochs cannot invalidate a ceremony. (4) Uncovered versions: in mode S the server re-encrypts them itself at commit (it can open both the head's and the new record's service wrap; S5 already opens the latter); in mode E a record flag declaring uncovered versions deleted, or an accepted quiet window.

findings.title: RemoveIdentity no longer revokes at replicas: a removed key stays an authorized client of every replica (and a decrypting reader) until a group admin rotates, and the operator has no remedy
findings.detail: Today server.rs remove_identity -> store.remove_identity_with_rotations cascades group_acl and rotates, and replicas' apply rule 2 (ACL wholesale) denies the key on its next request. New (3.6): RemoveIdentity(K) deletes the registry row and the authoritative node stops serving K at transport level, but K stays (K, r) in head.acl of every group with a valid wrap. K connects to any replica (replicas admit anyone and authorize from the mirrored ACL, protocol.md section 7); P5 forbids taking a roster from the server; so K gets plaintext for every group it was in and keeps decrypting every new push. The party with the RemoveIdentity power cannot end it; the group admin may be K itself or offline. Risk #3 covers only 'a removed replica', not removed identities as clients of other replicas (a departed human, a decommissioned CI key). Stranding side effect: S1 ('keys are registered') plus G3 (readers(rec) superset of readers(head) for acl epochs) means every later acl epoch of every group K was in carries an unregistered key and is refused, so the admin cannot even add a reader without a full rotate first; if K was the only admin, a ceremony.
findings.fix: Add a server-attested denylist to sync: manifest and Group messages carry revoked: [endpoint_id] (registry removals); replica authorization = chain ACL minus revoked. Safe under the hostile-server model because denial cannot escalate and the server can already withhold. Keep stale_recipients and the admin prompt for the cryptographic half; scope S1's registration check to keys NOT already in head.acl.

findings.title: Recovery from a restored database silently revives kicks made after the restore point, and a hostile server can induce it
findings.detail: Section 5 builds the recovery acl from 'the group's chain' obtained from the server or the SQLite file, i.e. the restored one. E12 = rotate that kicked Z (M12); DB restored to E10 (Z reader, M10); operator builds recovery R with prev=hash(E10), epoch=now, 'pure membership fix, same M' from E10's acl. Z is back with a valid wrap of M10; replicas at E12 accept R (P2 re-root, epoch > 12) and re-authorize Z. Nobody decided to revive Z; G7's 'exactly like a brand-new reader' assumes an admin chose it. A hostile server wanting Z back only needs to present an old head to the operator.
findings.fix: The recovery tool MUST gather heads from every reachable replica (or accept an operator-supplied highest-known head) and refuse, or warn and default to rotate, when the restored head is not the maximum; record the highest superseded hash in the sync-reroot / epoch-submit audit rows.

findings.title: A race-losing sibling record wedges a replica until a backup-key ceremony; the fix is keyless
findings.detail: L (prev=H, epoch=H+1, admin A) loses the CAS to W (same prev and epoch, admin B). L is a valid extension of H. A replica at H that receives L (hostile or buggy server, or the losing client's retry path) accepts it; every real successor fails P2 and the only re-root is a backup-signed recovery. A withheld replica heals when the server is fixed; a wedged one never does. The design lists equivocation as a detectability residual but not this zero-cost, ceremony-to-fix consequence.
findings.fix: P2 addition, verifiable without a key: a replica MAY replace its head by a same-height sibling (same prev, same epoch, valid under all rules) when the authoritative node also presents an admin-signed descendant of that sibling; audit sync-fork with both hashes; never return to a hash it abandoned. Residual: a server that equivocated to the admins as well.

findings.title: Forks on the authoritative node are possible between the local submit path and a running server; 'no forks on the authoritative node' relies on process discipline
findings.detail: 'Service stopped' for db submit-epoch is advisory. If it runs while serve is up, each does its CAS in its own SQLite transaction; the only constraint is PRIMARY KEY (group_id, epoch). Recovery R (epoch=now) and the server's epoch 11 both insert with different PKs: two heads, both children of E10. Replicas see 11 then R (re-root) or R then 11 (refused) depending on delivery order; the store shows a fork the rules said cannot exist.
findings.fix: UNIQUE(group_id, prev) on group_epoch plus an explicit head row updated in the same transaction; the local path takes an exclusive lock (BEGIN IMMEDIATE) and refuses when a serve-held lock file is present.

findings.title: The chain does not bind the group name, and the AAD binds the name rather than group_id: a server can relabel chains between groups a replica reads
findings.detail: Records carry group_id only; secret_group.epoch_group_id is a server-side mapping; the Group message carries name; secret_aad(group, name, version, dek_gen) uses the name string. Replica X reads 'prod' (G_p) and 'staging' (G_s); the server serves G_s's chain under name 'prod'. X authorizes 'prod' clients from staging's ACL and shows staging's roster in GroupAcl. No plaintext leaks (DEK/AAD mismatch makes every Get fail) but authorization is mislabelled, and an offline auditor holding a chain cannot say which group it governs.
findings.fix: Put len(name)||name in the genesis layout and derive the AAD from group_id (see finding 1); replicas bind name -> group_id at first sight and refuse a change.

findings.title: Role hygiene gaps: pinned keys may appear in acl (G2 satisfiable by the offline backup key), zero-perm entries, service-rekey's submitter and its silent recipient removal
findings.detail: (a) Nothing forbids the backup or service public key (both in the record) from appearing in acl: an admin authors acl={backup_key: rwa} and drops itself; G2 is satisfied by a key that is offline by definition, so the group looks administered but nobody online can author, and A2's second clause ('a record signed by the service key or the backup key ... MUST be refused') contradicts its first once such an entry exists. (b) E1 admits perms=0 entries: members with no semantics, usable as hidden markers. (c) service-rekey is authored by the service key, which is not an EndpointId, so S2 ('submitter == author') cannot be satisfied and the design never says it is server-local. (d) service-rekey keeps M and drops the old service key from wraps, the exact 'revocation theatre' G3 forbids for readers; the threat row admits a rotate must follow, but nothing flags the group as stale meanwhile.
findings.fix: E-rule: keys(pinned) and keys(acl) MUST be disjoint; perms MUST be non-zero. service-rekey is server-local and audited as such (no wire path). After a service-rekey set stale_recipients on every group until a rotate lands.

findings.title: Attribution edges: put_sig stripping is undetectable, 'author of head' is the wrong last-membership-change, recovery audit rows lose the author
findings.detail: (a) sig/author on puts are optional; a hostile server (or a mode-S bug) drops them and serves the version as legacy-unsigned; a reader cannot distinguish 'the writer did not sign' from 'the server stripped it', so verified attribution degrades silently to server-attested created_by. (b) 'Who last changed membership = author of the head' names the service key when the head is a service-rekey (acl unchanged). (c) S2 lets a service admin submit a recovery; the epoch-submit audit row is attributed to the submitter, not the record's author (the backup key).
findings.fix: Per-group client-side 'expect signed' policy (no chain change) or a Secret.verified tri-state, with the server storing put_sig immutably. Define attribution as 'author of the latest record whose acl differs from its predecessor's'. Audit epoch-submit with author= in the target or outcome.

findings.title: GroupEpochs (any bit) discloses the full raw-key roster and kick history to write-only identities
findings.detail: Today GroupAcl/ListIdentityNames are admin-gated and endpoint ids service-admin-gated. GroupEpochs requires 'any bit on the group', so a w-only CI key can fetch the chain and learn every reader's and admin's key and who kicked whom. Risk #9 covers replicas and database files, not the wire.
findings.fix: Gate GroupEpochs on read (readers already get the roster via sync) and give writers only the head's (epoch, hash, dek_gen) for CAS purposes.

strengths: A2 anchors authorship in the PREVIOUS epoch's acl, which cleanly closes self-promotion and same-record admin grants.
G3 (any read removal is a rotate) plus the one-generation invariant makes 'revocation theatre' impossible for readers, with the reasoning spelled out.
G4 + R2 + R3 make a sabotaged backup wrap unrepresentable rather than merely detectable, checked at submit by a key-less party; this is the strongest argument for the DLEQ in the design.
S3 CAS under the store lock and P2 extend-only give exact replay and rollback detection within a chain; `at` is advisory and never used for acceptance.
The service-admin table in 3.6 is honest about what is lost, and keeping service admins as explicit admins where wire recovery is wanted is a good escape hatch.
The recovery epoch jump (max(head+1, now)) and its rationale for restored databases are correct as far as they go.
The 'what is NOT proven' list is explicit and accurate.
verdict: Within a single chain the rules hold: no sequence of well-formed epoch records lets a reader become admin, escapes the last-admin rule, replays an old record, or removes the backup wrap. The defects are at the chain's boundaries. (1) A replica or auditor has no trust anchor for genesis, and the design's own drop-and-resync advice lets a hostile server replace a group's entire chain, contradicting the headline threat-model claim; (2) a client-supplied genesis can pin an attacker's backup key, making the group creator its permanent chain root; (3) the 'allow' default is justified by remedies (surviving-admin kick, backup recovery) that a rogue admin can starve indefinitely with one-signature epochs and S4 coverage; (4) RemoveIdentity no longer revokes at replicas and the operator has no remedy. Findings 1-4 should be resolved before implementation; 5-11 are specification fixes. Not ready as-is, but the chain core is right and the fixes are local: pinned backup root + per-name tombstones + name binding; pinned-set check at genesis; stage decoupled from prev plus server-side liveness rules; a server-attested denylist for registry removals.
